speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Hey everybody, Peter Zion here coming to you from Colorado. It is the 17th of July and it is the last day of the Republican National Convention, which I've been watching pretty closely because the Republican Party is in flux.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: For those of you who've been watching me for a while, you know that I've been saying for a couple years, several years now, that we're in the late party structure for what is called the sixth party structure.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Basically, every generation or two, American politics goes into a period of flux where the factions that make up our parties move around.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And for the last few years, we've been in that process. It's happening for both of the parties, but the Republicans are further along, so it's been the one I've been following most closely.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Donald Trump is obviously part of this process and has been speeding it along.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And now with the convention, we're starting to get a pretty good idea of what the next possible iteration of the Republicans are.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Quick review. So most people associate the Republicans with the degree of social conservatism, international involvement, relatively hawkish positions on foreign affairs, especially military affairs, and a fairly pro-business outlook for businesses of all size.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Every plank of that is now being challenged and rewritten by Team Trump as American society, demographics, trade, technology, and everything else is evolving.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: It makes sense. Whether or not this new structure that's evolving is the one that is going to stick remains to be seen.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: But we now have a pretty good idea of what the Trump Republican Party would be.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Three big changes. The first one is a little bit of a surprise, a softer position on some social conservative issues like gays and abortion.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Basically, the Trump Party is now saying that these are issues that should be decided by the states rather than the national level.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And there's a lot of hardcore conservatives, social conservatives, who are really pretty unhappy with that.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: But Donald Trump is betting that his cult of personality-like hold over the Republican Party is going to be sufficient, that no one can outflank him.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And considering that he sailed to the nomination without even showing up at any of the primaries, that's probably a safe bet, at least for this election cycle.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: The second one, of course, is something that's near and dear to my heart, and it's a shift from international involvement to isolationism.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: The idea that the problems over there are problems over there.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: We should just stick over here, but still arm ourselves to the teeth.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: We saw a lot of this in Trump's first term, where he might talk tough on countries with Russia and China.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: But really, on every major issue, whether it's trade or security, he basically just let them do whatever they want.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: If it couldn't be negotiated and stuck to in a single afternoon of talks, he really wasn't interested.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: We saw that, of course, with Ukraine, and we've also seen it with trade policy with China, where we got this phase one trade deal, but then Trump couldn't bother to enforce it.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: So the Chinese basically just walked all over the United States as regards trade.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Things like that are definitely being codified into the Republican Party's new platform.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And then the third one has to do with business versus labor.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: For the past several decades, really going back to the 1930s, the Republican Party has always sided with the business community over labor.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: But one of the highlight speakers of the convention at this time was none other than the representative of the Teamsters Union,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: which is probably the most militant and throwback of America's unions.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And he talked about the Chamber of Commerce basically being a welfare club for businesses.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And this is something that was on the stage of the Republican National Convention.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: I mean, for a while there, I was wondering if I was watching the right convention.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: These are issues that are usually trumpeted by not just the Democrats, but the really leftist group of Democrats, like, say, the Squad.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And now it's becoming core of the Republican Party platform.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: In essence, we are entering a golden age for organized labor in the United States.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: The United States is in the process of doubling the size of its industrial plant.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Most of those jobs are blue collar.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And so they're very amenable to be organized into labor unions.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: The Teamsters, of course, are all for that.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And what the Trump Republican Party seems to be doing is basically ditching the entire business community and going whole hog towards organized labor.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And among the new things that are in the Republican Party's platform are basically starting to challenge things like right-to-work laws in places like the American South and Texas

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: that prevent or at least dissuade unions from forming in the first place.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: It's now the official Republican Party platform that that's a bad idea.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Now, will this new trifecta stick?

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: It's way too soon to tell.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And the old Reaganite and Lankonian Republicans are not dead yet.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: There were some hilarious moments on stage from my point of view.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Ron DeSantis, who ran for president, of course, governor of Florida, he was just angry.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And it was pretty obvious.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: But I would say that the highlight here for awkwardness goes to Nikki Haley,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: who came in second in the primaries against Donald Trump, still lost, of course.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: She came on stage to endorse Trump.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And not only was she booed when she showed up, but her endorsement speech was really awkward.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: It was kind of like a woman being asked to toast her ex-husband who had an affair with the secretary and was now marrying her.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: It was that level of awkwardness.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Anyway, Nikki Haley has already joined a think tank to reimagine what the next version of conservatism looks like in the United States

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: now that the old Republican Party is truly and well dead.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And Mike Pence has formed a think tank to do the same thing.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Now, I'm not suggesting that one of these three visions, Pence or Haley or Trump, is the one that's ultimately going to stick.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: But I'm just highlighting that right now for this election cycle, we have a very different Republican platform and a very different Republican Party.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Everything is still in flux.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: This is not the final form.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: We won't get that probably until the next presidential cycle.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And there's a lot of folks who have irons in the fire to try to figure out what that is going to be.
